The {{citation-formatter|Citation Formatter}} repairs the shapes the audit counted, and the {{bibliography-builder|Bibliography Builder}} assembles the list the citations imply. When the reference set needs generating, the {{reference-list-generator|Reference List Generator}} builds it, and the tone analyzer in this domain smooths the patched paragraphs.

faqs.q: Does this tool compare my text to a database?
faqs.a: No. It audits quoting mechanics inside your draft — quotes, citations, quote share — and never uploads or compares text. The similarity score from a service like Turnitin is a different measurement, and the scope note says so.

faqs.q: What is the quote share limit?
faqs.a: Fifteen percent is the published convention this tool measures against: the proportion of the draft made of quoted words. Your venue's rules override it; the number exists so the draft has a line to stand on.

faqs.q: What counts as a block quote?
faqs.a: Any quoted passage past forty words, by the published threshold. The tool marks it so you can set it as a displayed block with its citation, rather than hiding a long quote inside a paragraph.

faqs.q: Which citation shapes does the scan recognise?
faqs.a: Author-year parentheses, bracketed numbers, the words footnote and ibid, and see-references. It counts shapes rather than verifying them — a wrong citation in the right shape still passes, which is the scan's honest limit.

faqs.q: Why prepare if the checker runs anyway?
faqs.a: Because the similarity report only tells you what matched, after the grade is at stake. The prep audit shows the same causes earlier — unattributed quotes and heavy quote share — while fixing them costs nothing but a revision.

intro: The Writing Portfolio Builder turns a list of published pieces into a curated reading portfolio — grouped by genre, selected for range and recency, with a scaffold you can paste.
content:
A portfolio is a curation, not an archive, and this writing portfolio builder does the curating. Paste your pieces — one per line, each with its title, genre, outlet, year and word count — and the tool groups them by genre, counts the dated and placed pieces, flags the pieces from the last three years, and selects the reading portfolio: up to ten pieces, with a floor of six, chosen to show range across genres rather than depth in one. The scaffold beside the selection is the page's skeleton, ready to fill.

The pieces panel takes the lines. The plan panel shows the groups with their counts, the selection with the reason each piece earned its place, and the counts that matter: total pieces, genres represented, how many are dated, how many carry an outlet, and the age of the most recent. Scope and limits says the builder curates what you paste; it cannot read the pieces or judge their quality.

- Pieces: title, genre, outlet, year and word count, one per line.
- Groups: pieces clustered by genre, counts beside each.
- Selection: up to ten pieces, minimum six, chosen for range.
- Recency: pieces from the last three years flagged as recent.
- Scaffold: the portfolio page's skeleton, generated from the selection.
- Counts: total, genres, dated, placed, selected, most recent.

The curation is parsing and selection: each line is parsed into its parts, the groups form by genre, and the selection balances the genres while preferring recent, placed pieces — a published rule, not a vibe. The scaffold is the selection rendered as a page skeleton with slots for links and one-line pitches. The same list always produces the same portfolio, which makes re-runs after new publications a diff rather than a redo.

- The selection favours range; a specialist portfolio may want to override it.
- Quality is assumed; the tool counts, it does not read.
- Pieces without a year still count, but they weaken the recency story.
- The scaffold is a skeleton; the links and pitches are yours.
- Nothing is stored, so copy the plan before closing the page.

Choose the genre to lead with before you look at the pieces — the portfolio opens with the work you want more of, and the selection rule's range bias is a starting point, not a verdict. Then fill the recency gap the counts expose: a portfolio whose newest piece is four years old tells an editor the pipeline stopped, and one recent clip repairs more than three old ones. Write the one-line pitch per selected piece last, and make each pitch a claim about the writing rather than a summary of the piece — an editor reads ten pitches in a minute, and the pitches are where the portfolio sounds like you. Keep the total at the target of ten: a portfolio that exhausts its reader has failed as a reading experience, and the floor of six exists so a thin list does not pad itself.

The neighbours shape the page around the clips: the manuscript formatter gets a selected piece submission-ready, the word count tool verifies the pitch lengths, and the reading time estimator shows the portfolio's minutes. The text summarizer in this domain compresses an overlong piece description to its pitch.
howTo: Paste the pieces, one per line, with title, genre, outlet, year and words.
Read the groups, the selection and the counts.
Check the recency story and the genre spread.
Copy the scaffold and write the one-line pitches.
whenToUse: Use the writing portfolio builder when the clips exist and the curation is overdue. The {{manuscript-formatter|Manuscript Formatter}} prepares a selected piece for submission, and the {{reading-time-estimator|Reading Time Estimator}} shows the portfolio's cost in minutes. When a piece description runs long, the {{text-summarizer|Text Summarizer}} cuts it to pitch length, and the word count tool in this domain keeps the page honest.

faqs.q: What format does each piece need?
faqs.a: One line per piece with the title, genre, outlet, year and word count. The year may be left blank, but a portfolio without dates weakens its own recency story, and the counts panel shows the cost.

faqs.q: Why a floor of six and a target of ten?
faqs.a: Six is the minimum a reading portfolio needs to show range; ten is where a reader's attention reliably ends. The selection respects both, and a list that cannot reach six is a signal to write, not to pad.

faqs.q: How are the selected pieces chosen?
faqs.a: By a published rule: spread across genres, preferring pieces from the last three years and ones that carry an outlet. The reason each piece earned its place is shown in the plan, so the curation is visible.

faqs.q: Does the builder judge my writing?
faqs.a: No. It curates the metadata you paste — genres, dates, outlets — and reads none of the pieces. Quality is your editorial problem; range and recency are the tool's.

faqs.q: Is my list saved?
faqs.a: No. The groups, selection and scaffold are computed in the page from your lines, and nothing is stored; copy the plan before the tab closes.
